items.title: US lawmakers raise alarm at FAA decision to deploy aviation AI tool nationally
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - A group of two dozen House Democrats on Tuesday raised serious concerns about the Federal Aviation Administration decision to deploy a new AI tool to assist air traffic controllers nationwide on November 10, days before a major system failure.

The FAA in September began using a new software-based AI tool system in the Washington area that uses predictive analytics to improve how flights are managed after awarding an $875 million, 12-year contract to Air Space Intelligence.

The Democrats, led by Representative Rick Larsen of Washington, the ranking member of the House Transportation Committee, criticized the "sudden expansion of a largely untested system" and asked the FAA to answer a series of questions by November 30. "We have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion," the lawmakers wrote.

The system, dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART, uses data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.

The letter cited the nearly five-hour November 13 nationwide ground stop that led flights to be canceled for an estimated 1.5 million passengers due to an FAA telecom issue.

"The federal government is dealing with a crisis of confidence," the letter said. "Americans' faith in the aviation system is shaken. The opacity and inconsistency with which the FAA has handled the SMART rollout threatens to further undermine that trust."

The lawmakers want to know the data used by the FAA to validate SMART operations and what redundancies are in place to "ensure reliable ATC operations in the event of issues or outages impacting SMART."

The lawmakers also cited reports that the FAA may have retaliated against employees who raised safety concerns about SMART's rapid deployment.

The FAA declined comment and said it would respond directly to the lawmakers.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has called the tool essentially "dumb AI" and emphasized controllers remain in charge, not the software.

The system uses over 200 data streams, creates data visualizations, and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along but does not involve active management of planes in the sky.

items.title: US malls make a holiday comeback as shoppers seek more than deals
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US mall owners and retailers are betting they can draw online shoppers with an experience they can't get from their screens: a festive day out.

Restaurants, entertainment and shared experiences are becoming increasingly important to draw shoppers to malls, surveys show, pushing brands to offer in-store deals and revamp their outlets to make the trip worthwhile.

Some 84% of Americans planning to shop over Thanksgiving weekend expect to do so in a physical store, the highest share since 2019, according to a survey by the International Council of Shopping Centers. And about 55% of US holiday shoppers plan to visit an indoor mall this season, up from roughly 50% last year, according to a separate consumer survey by real estate investment company JLL.

Brian Daniel, 55, of Grand Rapids, Michigan, said most of his shopping shifted online after the pandemic, but he has recently returned to malls, drawn partly by the experience of shopping in person.

"When I go to the mall, I'm not just in and out. I make it an evening. Shopping, dining, and a movie," Daniel said. During the holidays, he said, the music, decorations and ability to browse for gifts add to the appeal.

Refreshments are increasingly part of the shopping trip, with about 21% of respondents to JLL's survey expecting to buy a drink or food on every trip this holiday season, up from 12% last year.

"(Shoppers are) gravitating towards malls because of the depth and breadth of opportunities to shop," said Paul Chase, president of lifestyle property management at JLL. "It's important to customers or shoppers that they're going to go where they get ... the best experience."

Consumers heading for the mall expect to spend $1,357 per head during the holiday season, about 23% more than the amount budgeted by those who do not plan to visit malls, the JLL survey showed.

Shoppers expect to spend 17.3% more on dining and entertainment and 16% more on food and decorations than in the past holiday season, while planned spending on gifts is up just 3.1%, the survey showed.

THE NEW MALLRATS

Younger consumers are helping drive the shift, increasingly treating malls as a place to socialize rather than simply shop, Simon Property Group (SPG.N) CEO Eli Simon told a real estate conference in September.

Shoppers also "want to go where the best restaurants are; they want to go where the entertainment is," said Stephen Yalof, CEO of Tanger, which owns 42 shopping centers across the US and Canada, most of them outlet centers.

To lure shoppers, retailers are bolstering their in-store mall assortments while offering new experiences.

Coach (TPR.N), for example, is for the first time selling its Tabby and New York collection handbags across its outlet stores. In prior years, shoppers could only find these bags, which typically cost hundreds of dollars, in Coach's full-price retail stores.

"We're providing access to these items wherever our customer chooses to shop. That's new," said Leigh Manheim Levine, president of Coach North America. The brand realized that Gen Z shoppers "were very confused when they saw Tabby on TikTok but they didn't see it in the store," she said.

Coach has also been "fast and furiously" opening in-store cafés, Levine said. In the past two months, it has doubled the number of Coach Coffee Shops in North America to eight locations — mostly in outlet malls with limited food and beverage options.

"Customers have so many choices today, so we have to keep earning their visits by offering something they can't get online," said Nata Dvir, chief merchandising officer at department store chain Macy's (M.N). She pointed to an on-site Levi's tailoring pop-up and a custom Ralph Lauren embroidery station.

Reporting by Aishwarya Venugopal in Bengaluru and Danielle Kaye in Los Angeles; Editing by Lisa Jucca

items.title: US farm secretary pledges to fight court order halting her religious emails
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins pledged on Tuesday to challenge a court ruling that ordered her to stop sending religious emails to employees from her official account.

"We're going to fight it all the way to the Supreme Court," Rollins said in an interview on Fox News.

Several USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees sued Rollins in May, arguing she had "adopted a practice of sending increasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce," including emails to staff on Christmas and Easter.

An Easter email from Rollins to staff read in part, "Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind," according to a copy seen by Reuters.

"And so like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for," the email continued.

The suit argued that Rollins' use of "our" and "we" to refer to the Christian faith amounted to establishing a religious preference within the agency.

On November 19, a US district judge ruled that Rollins "appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion."

Rollins "must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages," including ending religious communication if asked to do so by a colleague, said the ruling.

The administration of President Donald Trump has sought to expand the role of religion in the federal workplace, including by allowing employees to promote their religious beliefs.

The First Amendment of the US Constitution broadly prohibits the government from establishing a national religion.

Reporting by Leah Douglas in Washington, Editing by Franklin Paul and Nia Williams

items.title: US transportation secretary to testify before Congress on air traffic outage
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will testify next week before a Senate subcommittee to answer questions on the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop that led to more than 18,000 cancelled flights and disrupted travel for 1.5 million Americans.

Duffy will also face questions on Dec. 2 from the Senate Commerce aviation subcommittee on his request for $50 billion for air traffic control and airport modernization, the panel said Tuesday. Duffy boosted his request from $30 billion after the tech outage blamed on the installation of a single router at an FAA facility in Arkansas. The ground stop was the longest such incident since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.

Reporting by David Shepardson

items.title: US consumer confidence jumps to highest level in nearly two years
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US consumer confidence increased more than expected in November, touching its highest level in nearly two years, amid optimism over labor market conditions and the overall economy following this month's midterm elections.

The sharp improvement in confidence reported by the Conference Board on Tuesday was driven by respondents identifying as Democrats and Independents. Confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly.

President Donald Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress to Democrats in the November 3 elections, which were dominated by anger over the rising cost of living, blamed on tariffs on imports and the US-Israeli war with Iran. The Conference Board survey noted that "while consumers continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs, some comments cited hope for the general economy."

Economists viewed the surge in confidence as a good omen for the holiday shopping season, though the correlation between consumer spending and confidence is weak. Consumer spending has recorded two back-to-back quarters of robust growth even as confidence was in the doldrums.

"The headwinds and uncertainty generated by the midterm elections are no longer posing a risk to the economic outlook," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Time will tell whether the stock market's troubles with AI valuations will lead to a slowdown in real consumption spending, that is partly based on the wealth effect, in the final months of the year."

The Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped to 103.3 this month, the highest level since January 2025, from a slightly upwardly revised 91.9 in October. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the index at 92.5 following a previously reported 91.7 in October. It mirrored a similar improvement in the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey.

The rise reported by the Conference Board was across all age groups and generations. Consumers with higher household incomes saw the largest improvement in confidence.

"Write-in responses in November were slightly less negative than previous months," said Fergus McCormick, a senior economist at the Conference Board.

The share of consumers saying jobs were "plentiful" soared to 30.8, the highest reading since May 2025, from 26.2 in October. The proportion viewing jobs as "hard to get" fell to 18.4. That was the lowest level since October 2025 and was down from 21.4 in October. The survey's so-called labor market differential widened to 12.4 from 4.8 last month.

This measure closely correlates to the unemployment rate in the Labor Department's employment report. The decline coincided with an acceleration in job gains in recent months. Consumers were also more upbeat about the labor market over the next six months, which bodes well for a further decline in the jobless rate.

INFLATION EXPECTATIONS ELEVATED

The unemployment rate dropped from 4.5% in November last year to 4.1% in October, though part of the decrease has been due to a smaller labor force amid retirements and the White House's immigration crackdown. Nonetheless, signs of a strengthening labor market is likely to clear the way for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again beyond December's anticipated hike as it tries to bring inflation under control.

The Conference Board's one-year median inflation expectations eased to a still-high 4.5% from 4.7% in October.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower as the sharp rally in AI shares following the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang fizzled. The dollar slipped against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

Despite the lingering angst over higher prices, more consumers planned to purchase motor vehicles as well as major appliances over the next six months. Some economists continued to expect consumer spending to slow down in the fourth quarter in part because of inflation eroding wage gains.

More consumers planned to buy a house over the next six months, with the share rising to a seven-month high despite elevated mortgage rates and higher home prices.

A separate report from the Federal Housing Finance Agency showed single-family house prices increased 2.5% in the 12 months through September after advancing 2.4% in August.

Mortgage rates have increased by about 130 basis points since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, data from mortgage finance firm Freddie Mac showed. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.28% last week.

While the higher borrowing costs have dampened demand, house prices have maintained their upward trend because most homeowners have mortgage rates below 5%. That is discouraging some from selling their houses and contributing to a national housing shortage, especially of starter homes.

"We expect annual home price growth to slow to below 2% in the fourth quarter and to remain there until early 2028," said Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics. "Weaker demand due to high mortgage rates will weigh on prices, although we expect mortgage rates above 7% will also keep sellers to the sidelines."

items.title: US bill aims to clear hurdle to medication for people with opioid addiction
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - A pair of Democratic US lawmakers on Tuesday unveiled a bill aimed at improving access to buprenorphine, a medication that can effectively treat opioid addiction but is not commonly used.

The so-called BUPE for Recovery Act, authored by US Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and New York Representative Paul Tonko, is designed to remove a regulatory hurdle pharmacies face when ordering the drug, Heinrich's office told Reuters.

Drug distributors like McKesson (MCK.N) and Cardinal Health (CAH.N) are required to report suspicious orders of controlled substances to a US Drug Enforcement Administration-run database known as SORS. Flagging can result in orders being blocked.

Buprenorphine, often called bupe, is technically an opioid, and is among the drugs that must be reported, which addiction doctors have long bemoaned. "The treatment is flagged the same as the poison," Gregory Famiglio, a Pennsylvania-based addiction physician, said in an interview.

Order thresholds are not known to pharmacies, and fear of enforcement can discourage orders, experts say. A 2025 study by University of Texas researchers found that heightened monitoring led to rationing of buprenorphine and care interruptions.

Heinrich and Tonko's legislation would exempt bupe from such reporting for the duration of the US opioid public health emergency, first declared in 2017, and would require the government to study whether it needs to be re-included after.

Though the current congressional session is wrapping up, introducing the bill now "helps build awareness and momentum," a Heinrich spokesperson said.

A previous version of the bill stalled in 2024, but Democrats will control both chambers of Congress beginning January 3.

BROADER BARRIERS

Buprenorphine, shown to reduce cravings and overdose risk, has been on the market since 2002. But only 15% to 20% of Americans with addiction use medication — whether buprenorphine or other options like methadone — to treat their disease, recent US surveys have shown.

Experts attribute the low figures to stigma on the part of prescribing doctors and pharmacists, low reimbursement rates, and difficulty persuading people with addiction to get help.

Only 38.8% of US pharmacies were regularly dispensing buprenorphine as of 2023, a study by University of Southern California and UC Berkeley researchers found.

Some experts fear it will take more than legislation to get those numbers up. In the shadow of the opioid crisis, buprenorphine still carries the stigma of a substance that can be misused to get high, although academic and medical research has shown that is a rare occurrence.

"There's this fear of stocking opioids... and being implicated in overdoses," said Dima Qato, an associate professor of pharmacy at USC, and an author of the study.

items.title: US agency expects to screen 17.6 million air travelers over Thanksgiving week, down slightly
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The US Transportation Security Administration forecast on Tuesday it will screen 17.6 million air passengers during the weeklong Thanksgiving holiday travel period, down slightly from 2025.

The TSA screened about 18.1 million passengers in the seven-day Thanksgiving holiday period in 2025. The TSA expects to screen more than 3 million passengers on Sunday, which would be the first time this year it would top that figure.

The Federal Aviation Administration said separately it expects nearly 418,000 flights to operate over the nine-day holiday period it uses, the most in 16 years and exceeding the nearly 410,000 flights in the same period last year. The FAA forecasts 52,345 flights on Tuesday, the highest for any day during the period.

A nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop on November 13 attributed to the installation of a single router at a southern Arkansas FAA facility led to more than 18,000 flight cancellations and disrupted travel for more than 1 million people.

The White House has since assembled the Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team — which includes officials from the FAA, departments of Transportation and Defense, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence — to oversee travel issues.

The FAA also warned stormy weather could affect flights throughout the week.

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Rod Nickel

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: JD Vance's ties to prized Venezuelan oil contract under investigation by US Senate panel
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - A US Senate committee is investigating whether US Vice President JD Vance played a role in the awarding of a lucrative Venezuelan oil deal to commodities giant Vitol, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

The investigation follows an exclusive Reuters report that detailed a meeting between Vance and Vitol trader John Addison a week before the United States invaded Venezuela in January and captured authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro.

"I write today with serious concern that you may have used your position as Vice President to help a major political donor secure lucrative business opportunities involving Venezuelan oil," according to the letter, sent to Vance by Senator Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat.

Hassan will become chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January when the new Congress is seated. She's seeking a number of documents from Vance's office by December 14. Among them are communications between Vance or his staff and Addison or the trading firm.

The meeting between Vance and Addison happened in December 2025 during a trip Vance made to Montana's Yellowstone Club, an ultra-exclusive ski and golf resort, according to a person familiar with the matter. At the time, Addison was a gasoline trader for Vitol with no expertise in trading Venezuelan crude, according to Vitol. He retired from Vitol earlier this year.

Vance and Addison talked about Venezuela, according to the person with knowledge of the meeting, who was given an account of the discussion by Addison. Vance was particularly interested to know how quickly Venezuelan crude could be sold if the US hypothetically gained control of the country's oil supplies, the person said. Addison assured Vance that Vitol was well-placed to do that job.

Both Vance and Addison have denied having the meeting.

Hassan wrote in her letter: "Despite denials from your office and Mr. Addison, flight records place his private jet and your government plane at the same Montana airport on the day of the reported meeting."

In response to questions for this story, Vance's press secretary, Luke Schroeder, said in a statement: "The alleged airport meeting never happened."

Reuters did not specify, in the original report, that the meeting happened at the airport.

Vitol and Addison were not immediately available for comment.

Addison has confirmed to Reuters that on January 5 – two days after the operation that ousted Maduro and killed up to 100 people – US Energy Secretary Chris Wright called him at his desk in Houston with an irresistible offer.

President Donald Trump's administration was planning to start selling the South American OPEC nation's crude to global buyers to finance its coming political transition. Wright wanted to know from Addison if Vitol wanted the job.

The Department of Energy confirmed Wright called Addison on January 5 to discuss Venezuela.

Within days, Vitol and its rival trading firm Trafigura landed special licenses to sell Venezuela's oil, according to the two firms. The companies have since earned hundreds of millions of dollars marketing the crude, according to estimates by independent experts.

The United States handled more than $12 billion of Venezuela's oil revenue in the first nine months of this year, according to a report made public by the State Department earlier this month.

Addison had been an early backer of Vance, contributing $300,000 in 2022 to the Protect Ohio Values Political Action Committee to help Vance's successful bid for one of Ohio's US Senate seats, Federal Election Commission records show.

Later, Addison and his wife, Shannon, contributed $7 million in 2024 to political action committees to help secure Trump's second term in the White House, according to Federal Election Commission records.

Reporting By Tim McLaughlin; Editing by Anna Driver
